title: Participle adjectives and compound adjectives
subtitle: a broken plate / well-behaved children
summary: Use -ing and -ed participles as adjectives, place them correctly around the noun, and build compound adjectives.

lesson.heading: Participle adjectives
lesson.text: Some -ing forms (present participles) and -ed forms (past participles) of verbs work as adjectives. Most of them can go before the noun they describe or after a linking verb.

examples.text: I found this **broken** plate in the kitchen cupboard.
My mother seemed **delighted** with the present.

lesson.heading: Reduced relative clauses after the noun
lesson.text: Many participle adjectives can follow a noun directly when they identify or define it. This works like a defining relative clause, which is why these are often called 'reduced relatives'.

examples.text: We had to pay for the rooms **used**.
My watch was among the things **taken**.
Please answer the questions on the sheet **provided**.

lesson.note: Rarely used before the noun: applying, caused, found, included, provided, taken, used.

lesson.heading: After the noun or before it

left.label: After the noun
examples: Steps are being taken to solve the problems **identified**.

right.label: Before the noun
examples: Steps are being taken to solve the **identified** problems.

lesson.note: Also affected, alleged, allocated, broken, chosen, infected, interested, resulting, stolen.

lesson.heading: that and those + participle adjective
lesson.text: In formal English, that and those can act as pronouns in front of a participle adjective - that for a singular or uncountable noun, those for a plural noun or for people.

examples.text: The flour is of a higher quality than **that produced** by other varieties of wheat.
The touchscreens perform less well than **those manufactured** elsewhere.
Here is some advice for **those preparing** to go on holiday.

lesson.heading: Compound adjectives with a participle
rows: She seems to live on **ready-made** meals.
He's the **longest-serving** employee in the company.
I hope it will be a **money-making** enterprise.
Did it really happen, or was it a **made-up** story?

lesson.heading: Participles that only live in compounds
lesson.text: Some participle adjectives make no sense on their own: without the adverb or noun in front, the meaning is incomplete. So we can't say 'behaved children' or 'a making enterprise'.

examples.text: The school is **well-resourced**, with sufficient books and computers.

lesson.note: Also New York-based, Paris-born, brick-built, easy-going, peace-keeping, long-lasting, good-looking, home-made, hair-raising, sweet-smelling, strange-sounding, soft-spoken, sour-tasting.

lesson.text: Many compound adjectives contain no participle at all: The problem is **short-term**. / It was just a **small-scale** project.

exercises.prompt: Please answer the questions on the sheet ___.
exercises.explanation: Provided defines which sheet, and it is not used before the noun.
Included follows the noun - we don't say 'the included flights'.

exercises.statement: My watch was among the taken things.
exercises.explanation: My watch was among the things taken. Taken is one of the participle adjectives that cannot go before the noun.

exercises.prompt: ___ visitors can buy a booklet with further information.
exercises.explanation: Interested can go before the noun (or after it: visitors interested in ...).

exercises.prompt: Steps are being taken by telephone engineers to solve the problems ___.
exercises.explanation: Identified can follow the noun as a reduced relative (= the problems that have been identified).

exercises.prompt: I didn't want to be on TV but the ___ publicity was good for business.
exercises.explanation: Resulting works before or after the noun (the publicity resulting was also possible).

exercises.prompt: Just before serving the pasta, sprinkle over any cheese ___.
exercises.explanation: Remaining can follow the noun here, or come before it: any remaining cheese.

exercises.prompt: Organic oranges contain 30% more vitamin C than ___ conventionally.
exercises.explanation: Those stands for the plural noun oranges before the participle adjective.

exercises.prompt: The President's salary is 25 times higher than ___ by the average citizen.
exercises.explanation: Salary is singular, so we use that, not those.

exercises.prompt: Match each description with the compound adjective that says the same thing.

pairs.left: The company is organised from New York.
The school has all the books and computers it needs.
The whole experience made me tense and worried.
The changes will have a major influence on a large number of people.
The discussions dealt with a great variety of topics.
When I last saw him he had a beard, but now he has none.

exercises.prompt: The advertisements for the new car are very ___.
exercises.explanation: Noun + -ing participle: the advertisements catch your eye.

exercises.prompt: Can each participle adjective also be used before the noun, or only after it?
